english: So loveliness reigned, and stillness, and together they made the shape of loveliness itself, a form that life had left; solitary, like a pool at evening, far off, seen from a train window, vanishing so quickly that the pool, pale in the evening, is hardly robbed of its solitude, though it has once been seen. Loveliness and stillness clasped hands in the bedroom; and among the shrouded jugs and sheeted chairs, even the prying of the wind, and the soft noses of the clammy sea airs, rubbing, snuffling, repeating and repeating their questions—“Will you fade? Will you perish?”—hardly disturbed the peace, the indifference, the air of pure integrity, as if the question they asked scarcely needed an answer: we remain.

english: As she lurched (for she rolled like a ship at sea) and leered (for her eyes never fell on anything directly, but only with a sidelong glance that asked to be spared the scorn and anger of the world—she was witless, she knew it), as she clutched the banisters and hauled herself upstairs and rolled from room to room, she sang. Rubbing the glass of the long mirror and leering sideways at her swaying figure, she let a sound come from her lips—something that had perhaps been cheerful on the stage twenty years before, had been hummed and danced to, but now, coming from this toothless, bonneted caretaker, was robbed of meaning. It was like the voice of witlessness, of humor, of persistence itself, trodden down but springing up again; so that as she lurched along, dusting, wiping, she seemed to be saying how it was all one long sorrow and trouble, how it was getting up and going to bed again, and getting things out and putting them away again. It had not been easy or cozy, this world she had known for close on seventy years. She was bowed down with weariness. How long, she asked, creaking and groaning on her knees under the bed, dusting the boards, how long is it to go on? But she hobbled to her feet again, pulled herself up, and again, with her sidelong leer that slipped and turned aside even from her own face and her own sorrows, stood and gaped in the glass, smiling at nothing, and began again the old amble and hobble, taking up mats, putting down china, looking sideways in the glass—as if, after all, she had her consolations; as if some incorrigible hope really did twine itself around her dirge. There must have been visions of joy at the washtub, say, with her children (though two had been born out of wedlock and one had deserted her), or at the pub, drinking, or turning over odds and ends in her drawers. There must have been some break in the dark, some channel in the depths of obscurity through which enough light came to twist her face into a grin in the glass, and make her, turning to her work again, mumble out the old music-hall song. Meanwhile the mystics, the visionaries, walked the beach, stirred a puddle, looked at a stone, and asked themselves, “What am I?” “What is this?”—and suddenly an answer was granted them (what it was they could not say), so that they were warm in the frost and had comfort in the desert. But Mrs. McNab went on drinking and gossiping as before.

Mens hun gnubbede glasset i det lange spejl og skelede sidelæns til sin vaklende skikkelse, lod hun en lyd komme fra sine læber — noget, der måske havde været muntert på scenen tyve år før, var blevet nynnet og danset til, men nu, når det kom fra denne tandløse, huebærende vicevært, var berøvet al mening. Det var som enfoldighedens, humorens, selve udholdenhedens stemme, nedtrampet, men skydende op igen; så at hun, mens hun slingrede af sted og støvede af og tørrede, syntes at sige, hvordan det hele var én lang sorg og møje, hvordan det var at stå op og gå i seng igen og tage ting frem og lægge dem på plads igen. Det havde ikke været let eller hyggeligt, denne verden hun havde kendt i næsten halvfjerds år. Hun var bøjet af træthed. Hvor længe, spurgte hun, mens hun knirkede og stønnede på knæ under sengen og støvede gulvbrædderne af, hvor længe skal det blive ved? Men hun humpede op på benene igen, trak sig op og stod atter med sit sidelange skel, der gled og vendte sig bort selv fra hendes eget ansigt og hendes egne sorger, og gloede i spejlet, smilende til ingenting, og begyndte påny det gamle slæbende humpetrav, tog måtter op, stillede porcelæn på plads, så sidelæns i spejlet — som om hun trods alt havde sine trøster; som om et uforbederligt håb virkelig snoede sig om hendes klagesang. Der må have været glædesbilleder ved vaskebaljen, for eksempel, med hendes børn (skønt to var født uden for ægteskab, og én havde forladt hende), eller på kroen, når hun drak, eller når hun rodede i det løse i sine skuffer. Der må have været et brud i mørket, en kanal i dybet af tilsløring, gennem hvilken lys nok kom til at fortrække hendes ansigt til et grin i spejlet og få hende til, mens hun vendte sig mod sit arbejde igen, at mumle den gamle varietésang. Imens vandrede mystikerne, de synske, på stranden, rørte i en vandpyt, så på en sten og spurgte sig selv: »Hvad er jeg?« »Hvad er dette?« — og pludselig blev dem givet et svar (hvad det var, kunne de ikke sige), så de var varme i frosten og havde trøst i ørkenen. english: Yet however deeply the house might slumber and sleep, later that summer ominous sounds reached it, like hammer blows falling in a slow rhythm, muffled on felt. Their repeated shocks loosened the shawl further still and cracked the teacups. Every so often a glass tinkled in the cupboard, as though some giant voice had screamed so loud in its agony that even the tumblers standing inside a cupboard shook too. Then silence fell once more. And then, night after night—and sometimes in the full light of noon, when the roses were bright and the light printed its shape plainly on the wall—there seemed to drop into this silence, this indifference, this wholeness, the thud of something falling.

english: That season, people who had gone down to walk the beach and ask the sea and sky what message they carried, or what vision they confirmed, found something new to consider. Among the familiar signs of heaven’s generosity—sunset on the sea, the pale dawn, the rising moon, fishing boats against the moon, children throwing handfuls of grass at one another—there was something that did not fit with all this gaiety and calm. There was, for instance, a gray ship, the color of ash, that silently appeared and was gone; there was a purple stain on the smooth sea, as though something underneath had boiled and bled out of sight. These things broke into a scene built to call up the loftiest thoughts and lead to the most reassuring conclusions, and they stopped the walkers in their tracks. It was hard to pass over them calmly, to cancel out what they meant in the landscape; hard to keep walking by the sea and marveling that the beauty outside mirrored the beauty within.

english: She meant no harm by it. The family wouldn’t come, never again, some said, and maybe the house would be sold at Michaelmas, the autumn quarter day. So Mrs. McNab bent down and picked a bunch of flowers to carry home. While she dusted, she set them on the table. She liked flowers. It seemed a shame to let them go to waste. Say the house was sold (and she stood, hands on hips, before the looking glass)—well, it would need seeing to, that it would. All these years it had stood there with nobody in it. The books and things were moldy, what with the war and help being so hard to come by; the place hadn’t been cleaned the way she’d have wanted. It would take more than one pair of hands to set it right now. She was too old for it. Her legs hurt. Every one of those books ought to be laid out on the grass in the sun; plaster had come down in the hall; the drainpipe over the study window had got blocked and let the rain in; the carpet was completely ruined. But people should come and see for themselves; they should’ve sent someone down to look. There were clothes in the cupboards, after all; they’d left clothes in every bedroom. What was she meant to do with them? The moth was in them—Mrs. Ramsay’s things. Poor lady! She’d never need _them_ again. She was dead, they said; years ago, in London. Here was the old gray cloak she used to garden in (Mrs. McNab ran her fingers over it). She could see her now, as she came up the drive with the washing, bent over her flowers (a pitiful sight the garden was now, run wild, rabbits scuttling out at you from the beds)—could see her in that gray cloak with one of the children by her side. There were boots and shoes; there was a brush and comb left lying on the dressing table, for all the world as if she meant to be back tomorrow. (She’d died very sudden at the end, they said.) Once they’d been going to come, but they put it off, what with the war and traveling being so hard these days; and all these years they’d never come; only sent her money; never wrote, never came, and expected to find everything just as they left it, ah dear! Why, the drawers in the dressing table were stuffed full (she pulled them open)—handkerchiefs, scraps of ribbon. Yes, she could see Mrs. Ramsay, as she came up the drive with the washing.
danish_before_fix: Hun mente intet ondt med det. Familien ville ikke komme, aldrig mere, sagde nogle, og måske blev huset solgt ved mikkelsdag, efterårets kvartalsdag. Så fru McNab bøjede sig og plukkede en buket blomster til at tage med hjem. Mens hun støvede af, satte hun dem på bordet. Hun holdt af blomster. Det var jo synd at lade dem gå til spilde. Hvis nu huset blev solgt (og hun stod med hænderne i siden foran spejlet) — ja, så skulle der gøres noget ved det, det skulle der så. I alle de år havde det stået her uden et menneske i. Bøgerne og tingene var muggent, hvad med krigen og så svært, som det var at få hjælp; stedet var ikke blevet gjort rent, som hun gerne ville have. Der skulle mere end ét par hænder til at få det i orden nu. Hun var for gammel til det. Hun havde ondt i benene. Hver eneste af de bøger burde lægges ud på græsset i solen; kalken var faldet ned i gangen; nedløbsrøret over studerekammerets vindue var stoppet til og lod regnen komme ind; tæppet var fuldstændig ødelagt. Men folk burde komme og se selv; de burde have sendt nogen ned for at kigge. Der var jo tøj i skabene; de havde efterladt tøj i hvert eneste soveværelse. Hvad skulle hun gøre med det? Møllet var i det — fru Ramsays ting. Stakkels dame! Hun skulle aldrig få brug for _dem_ mere. Hun var død, sagde de; for år siden, i London. Her var den gamle grå kappe, hun plejede at gå i, når hun var i haven (fru McNab strøg fingrene hen over den). Hun kunne se hende for sig, som hun kom op ad indkørslen med vasketøjet, bøjet over sine blomster (en ynkelig tilstand haven var i nu, groet til, kaniner, der fór frem fra bedene på en) — kunne se hende i den grå kappe med et af børnene ved sin side. Der var støvler og sko; der var en børste og en kam, der lå på toiletbordet, ganske som om hun regnede med at være tilbage i morgen. (Hun var død meget pludseligt til sidst, sagde de.) Engang havde de tænkt sig at komme, men de udsatte det, hvad med krigen og så svært, som det var at rejse i disse tider; og i alle de år var de aldrig kommet; havde kun sendt hende penge; aldrig skrevet, aldrig kommet, og forventede at finde alting, som de havde forladt det, ak ja! Skufferne i toiletbordet var jo propfulde (hun trak dem op) — lommetørklæder, stumper af bånd. Ja, hun kunne se fru Ramsay for sig, som hun kom op ad indkørslen med vasketøjet.

english: The house had been left; the house stood deserted. Now that life had gone out of it, it was left like a shell on a sand dune, to fill up with dry grains of salt. The long night seemed to have begun; the trivial little airs that nibbled, the damp breaths that fumbled, seemed to have won the day. Rust had got into the saucepan, and the mat had rotted. Toads had nosed their way indoors. The shawl swung to and fro, idly, without purpose. In the larder a thistle forced its way up between the tiles. Swallows built nests in the drawing room; straw littered the floor; plaster came down by the shovelful; the beams showed through; rats carried off odds and ends to gnaw behind the wooden paneling. Tortoiseshell butterflies broke out of their chrysalises and beat their lives away against the windowpane. Poppies seeded themselves among the dahlias; long grass waved on the lawn; huge artichokes towered over the roses; a fringed carnation bloomed among the cabbages. And the soft tapping of a weed against the window had turned, on winter nights, into a drumming of sturdy trees and thorny briars, and in summer these made the whole room green.

Den lange nat syntes at være begyndt; de ubetydelige små vindpust, der nippede, de fugtige åndedrag, der famlede, syntes at have vundet dagen. Rust var kommet i kasserollen, og måtten var rådnet. Tudser havde snuset sig vej indendørs. Sjalet svingede frem og tilbage, ørkesløst, uden formål. I spisekammeret trængte en tidsel sig op mellem fliserne. Svaler byggede rede i dagligstuen; halm lå strøet over gulvet; kalk faldt ned i skovlfulde; bjælkerne viste sig; rotter slæbte ting og sager af sted for at gnave bag træpanelet. Takvingede sommerfugle brød ud af deres puppehylstre og slog deres liv ihjel mod ruden. Valmuer såede sig selv blandt georginerne; langt græs bølgede på plænen; kæmpestore artiskokker rejste sig over roserne; en frynset nellike blomstrede blandt kålen. Takvingede sommerfugle brød ud af deres puppehylstre og slog deres liv ihjel mod ruden. Valmuer såede sig selv blandt georginerne; langt græs bølgede på plænen; kæmpestore artiskokker rejste sig over roserne; en frynset nellike blomstrede blandt kålen. Og den bløde banken fra et ukrudt mod vinduet var på vinternætter blevet til en trommen af kraftige træer og tornede brombærranker, og om sommeren gjorde de hele værelset grønt.

english: What power was there now to stop the fertility of nature, its blind indifference? Mrs. McNab’s dream of a lady, a child, a plate of milk soup? That had flickered across the walls like a patch of sunlight and was gone. She had locked the door and left. One woman couldn’t manage it, she said. They never sent word. They never wrote. Up there, things were rotting in the drawers—a shame to leave them like that, she said. The whole place had gone to rack and ruin. Only the beam from the Lighthouse entered the rooms, for a moment at a time, throwing its sudden stare across bed and wall in the winter dark and gazing without concern at the thistle and the swallow, the rat and the straw. There was nothing left to stand against them, nothing to tell them no. So let the wind blow. Let the poppy sow itself, and the carnation mate with the cabbage. Let the swallow nest in the drawing room, the thistle shoulder the tiles aside, the butterfly sun itself on the faded chintz of the armchairs. Let the broken glass and china lie out on the lawn, overgrown and tangled with grass and wild berries.

english: And now, as though all the cleaning and scrubbing, the scything and mowing, had been drowning it out, there rose up that half-heard melody, that broken, fitful music that the ear half catches and then lets slip. A bark, a bleat—irregular, now and then, yet somehow connected. An insect humming, cut grass quivering—separate, yet somehow belonging together. A dor beetle’s drone, a wheel’s squeak, loud, soft, but mysteriously related. The ear strains to bring them together, and is always just about to make them into a harmony; but they are never quite heard, never fully harmonized, and at last, in the evening, the sounds die out one by one, the harmony wavers, and silence falls. As the sun set, the sharp edges faded, and quiet rose like a mist and spread; the wind dropped; the world shook itself loosely down to sleep—dark here, with no light in it except what filtered green through the leaves, or lay pale on the white flowers by the window.

english: Alone at the long table among the clean cups (Nancy had gone out again), she felt shut off from everyone else, fit only to keep on watching, asking and wondering. The house, the place, the morning all felt like strangers. She had no ties here, she felt, no connection with any of it; anything at all might happen. And whatever did happen—a footstep outside, a voice calling out (“It’s not in the cupboard, it’s on the landing!” somebody shouted)—came as a question, as if the thread that normally held things together had been snipped and they were drifting about, up here, down there, away, any old how. How pointless it all was, how chaotic, how unreal, she thought, gazing at her empty coffee cup. Mrs. Ramsay dead; Andrew killed; Prue dead as well—she could say it over as often as she liked and it woke no feeling in her. And here we all are, gathered in a house like this, on a morning like this, she said, looking out of the window. It was a lovely, still day.

Huset, stedet, morgenen føltes alle som fremmede. Hun havde ingen bånd her, følte hun, ingen forbindelse til noget af det; hvad som helst kunne ske. Og hvad der end skete — et fodtrin udenfor, en stemme der råbte (»Den er ikke i skabet, den er på repos!« råbte nogen) — kom det som et spørgsmål, som om den tråd, der normalt holdt tingene sammen, var klippet over, og de drev rundt, heroppe, dernede, væk, hulter til bulter. english: She brought herself a chair. With her neat, precise, old-maidish movements she set up her easel at the edge of the lawn—not too near Mr. Carmichael, but near enough to be under his protection. Yes, this must have been the very spot where she had stood ten years ago. There was the wall, there the hedge, there the tree. It was a question of how those masses related to one another. She had carried that question in her head all these years. And now it seemed that the answer had come to her: she knew what she wanted to do.

Det drejede sig om, hvordan disse masser forholdt sig til hinanden. Hun havde båret på det spørgsmål i sit hoved alle de år. Og nu syntes det, som om svaret var kommet til hende: hun vidste, hvad hun ville gøre.

english: But with Mr. Ramsay bearing down on her, she could do nothing at all. Each time he drew near—he was pacing up and down the terrace—ruin drew near, chaos drew near. Painting was impossible. She bent down; she turned away; she picked up this rag; she squeezed that tube. But all it did was keep him off for a moment. He made it impossible for her to get anything done. For if she gave him the slightest opening—if he caught her free for a moment, or glancing his way for a moment—he would be upon her, saying, as he had last night, “You find us much changed.” Last night he had stood up, come to a halt in front of her, and said just that. The six children, whom they used to nickname after the Kings and Queens of England—the Red, the Fair, the Wicked, the Ruthless—had all sat there, mute and staring, yet she had felt how furious they were underneath. Kind old Mrs. Beckwith had said something sensible. But it was a house full of passions that had nothing to do with one another—she had felt that the whole evening. And on top of all this chaos Mr. Ramsay had stood up, pressed her hand, and said, “You will find us much changed,” and not one of them had stirred or spoken; they had sat there as if they had no choice but to let him say it. Only James (certainly the Sullen one) glowered at the lamp, and Cam wound her handkerchief round and round her finger. Then he reminded them that tomorrow they were going to the Lighthouse. They were to be ready in the hall at half past seven sharp. Then, with his hand on the door, he paused and swung round on them. Didn’t they want to go? he demanded. If they had dared to say no (he had some reason for wanting it), he would have hurled himself tragically backward into the bitter waters of despair. He had such a talent for gesture. He looked like a king in exile. James said yes, doggedly. Cam faltered more miserably. Yes, oh yes, they would both be ready, they said. And it came to her that this was what tragedy was—not funeral palls, dust and the shroud, but children forced into things, their spirits subdued. James was sixteen, and Cam seventeen, perhaps. She had looked around for someone who was not there—for Mrs. Ramsay, presumably. But there was only kind Mrs. Beckwith, leafing through her sketches under the lamp. Then, tired as she was, her mind still rising and sinking with the sea, the taste and smell that a place has after a long absence taking hold of her, the candles flickering before her eyes, she had lost hold of herself and gone under. It was a marvelous starlit night; they heard the waves as they climbed the stairs; the moon took them by surprise, huge and pale, as they passed the landing window. She had fallen asleep at once.

Det var umuligt at male. Hun bøjede sig ned; hun vendte sig bort; hun tog denne klud op; hun klemte på den tube. Men alt, hvad det gjorde, var at holde ham fra livet et øjeblik. Han gjorde det umuligt for hende at få noget fra hånden. For hvis hun gav ham den mindste åbning — hvis han fangede hende fri et øjeblik eller med et blik i hans retning et øjeblik — ville han være over hende og sige, som han havde gjort i går aftes: »De finder os meget forandrede.« I går aftes havde han rejst sig, var standset foran hende og havde sagt netop det. De seks børn, som de plejede at give tilnavne efter Englands konger og dronninger — den Røde, den Lyse, den Onde, den Hensynsløse — havde alle siddet der, stumme og stirrende, og alligevel havde hun mærket, hvor rasende de var nedenunder. Rare gamle fru Beckwith havde sagt noget fornuftigt. Men det var et hus fuldt af lidenskaber, der intet havde med hinanden at gøre — det havde hun følt hele aftenen. Og oven i al den uorden havde hr. Ramsay rejst sig, trykket hendes hånd og sagt: »De vil finde os meget forandrede,« og ikke en af dem havde rørt sig eller sagt noget; de havde siddet der, som om de ikke havde andet valg end at lade ham sige det. Kun James (bestemt den Mut) havde stirret vredt på lampen, og Cam havde viklet sit lommetørklæde rundt og rundt om fingeren. Så havde han mindet dem om, at i morgen skulle de til Fyret. De skulle stå klar i entréen klokken præcis halv otte. Så, med hånden på døren, var han standset og havde vendt sig brat mod dem. Ville de ikke af sted? krævede han at vide. Hvis de havde vovet at sige nej (han havde sine grunde til at ville det), ville han have kastet sig tragisk baglæns ned i fortvivlelsens bitre vande. Han havde sådan en begavelse for gestus. Han så ud som en konge i landflygtighed. James sagde ja, stædigt. Cam tøvede mere ynkeligt. Jo, å jo, de ville begge være klar, sagde de. Og det gik op for hende, at det var det, tragedie var — ikke ligklæder, støv og svøb, men børn tvunget ind i tingene, deres sind kuet. James var seksten og Cam sytten, måske. Hun havde set sig omkring efter en, der ikke var der — efter fru Ramsay, formodentlig. Men der var kun rare fru Beckwith, der bladrede i sine skitser under lampen. Så, træt som hun var, med sindet der stadig steg og sank med havet, med den smag og lugt, et sted har efter lang tids fravær, der tog hende i besiddelse, med de blafrende stearinlys for øjnene, havde hun mistet fodfæstet og var sunket. Det var en vidunderlig stjerneklar nat; de hørte bølgerne, mens de gik op ad trappen; månen overraskede dem, kæmpestor og bleg, da de passerede vinduet på repos. Hun var faldet i søvn med det samme.

english: She fixed her clean canvas firmly on the easel as a barrier—a fragile one, but solid enough, she hoped, to keep Mr. Ramsay and his demands at bay. Whenever his back was turned she did her best to look at her picture—that line there, that mass there. But it was hopeless. He might be fifty feet away, he might not say a word to you, might not so much as see you, yet he seeped into everything, he won out, he forced himself on you. He altered everything. The color was lost to her; the lines were lost to her; even with his back to her all she could think was, He’ll be on me in a moment, wanting—something she felt she was unable to give. She put down one brush and picked up another. When were those children going to come? When would they all be gone? she fretted. That man, she thought, her anger mounting, never gave anything; that man only took. Whereas she would be made to give. Mrs. Ramsay had given. Giving and giving and giving, she had died—and left all this behind. Honestly, she was angry with Mrs. Ramsay. Her brush trembling a little between her fingers, she looked at the hedge, the step, the wall. It was all Mrs. Ramsay’s doing. She was dead. And here was Lily, forty-four years old, wasting her time, unable to do anything, standing there pretending to paint—playing at the one thing that was not to be played at—and it was all Mrs. Ramsay’s fault. She was dead. The step she used to sit on was empty. She was dead.

Hver gang han vendte ryggen til, gjorde hun sit bedste for at se på sit billede — den linje dér, den masse dér. Men det var håbløst. Han kunne være halvtreds fod væk, han behøvede ikke sige et ord til én, ikke så meget som se én, og alligevel sivede han ind i alt, han sejrede, han trængte sig på. Han ændrede alt. Farven var tabt for hende; linjerne var tabt for hende; selv med ryggen til hende kunne hun kun tænke: Han er over mig om et øjeblik og vil have — noget, hun følte sig ude af stand til at give. Hun lagde den ene pensel fra sig og tog en anden. Hvornår kom de børn? Hvornår var de alle væk? bekymrede hun sig. Den mand, tænkte hun, mens hendes vrede steg, gav aldrig noget; den mand tog bare. Mens hun ville blive nødt til at give. Fru Ramsay havde givet. Givet og givet og givet var hun død — og havde efterladt alt dette. Helt ærligt, hun var vred på fru Ramsay. Med penslen let skælvende mellem fingrene så hun på hækken, trinnet, muren. Det var alt sammen fru Ramsays skyld. Hun var død. Og her stod Lily, fireogfyrre år gammel, og spildte sin tid, ude af stand til at gøre noget, stod og lod, som om hun malede — legede med det ene, man ikke skulle lege med — og det var alt sammen fru Ramsays skyld. Hun var død. Trinnet, hun plejede at sidde på, var tomt. Hun var død.

english: Mr. Ramsay let out the fullest of sighs. He waited. Wasn’t she going to say anything? Couldn’t she see what he wanted from her? Then he told her he had a particular reason for wanting to go to the Lighthouse. His wife used to send things to the men there. The lighthouse keeper had a son, a poor boy with a tubercular hip. He gave a deep sigh. He gave a meaningful sigh. What Lily wished, and all she wished, was that this enormous flood of grief, this hunger for sympathy that could never be satisfied, this demand that she hand herself over to him completely—and even then he would have sorrows enough to keep her supplied forever—would leave her alone, would be turned aside (she kept looking at the house, hoping someone would interrupt) before its current swept her away.

english: Mr. Ramsay smiled instead. The pall, the drapes, the infirmities all dropped off him. Ah yes, he said, raising his foot so she could look, these were first-rate boots. Only one man in England could make boots like that. Boots, he said, were among the chief curses of the human race. “Bootmakers,” he exclaimed, “make it their business to cripple and torture the human foot.” No people on earth were more stubborn and contrary. He had spent the better part of his youth getting boots made as boots ought to be made. She would please notice (up went his right foot, then his left) that she had never before seen boots of quite that shape. And the leather was the finest in the world. Most leather was mere brown paper and cardboard. Pleased with himself, he gazed at his foot, which was still in the air. They had arrived, she felt, at a sunny island where peace made its home, where sanity was in charge and the sun never stopped shining: the blessed island of good boots. She felt a warmth toward him. “Now let’s see whether you can tie a knot,” he said. He brushed aside her feeble method with scorn and demonstrated his own invention. Tie it once and it would never come undone. Three times he knotted her shoe; three times he unknotted it.

Der var kun én mand i England, der kunne lave støvler som dem. Støvler, sagde han, var blandt menneskeslægtens værste plager. »Skomagere,« udbrød han, »gør det til deres sag at lemlæste og pine den menneskelige fod.« Intet folk på jorden var mere stædige og genstridige. Han havde brugt det meste af sin ungdom på at få lavet støvler, som støvler burde laves. Hun ville være så venlig at bemærke (op gik hans højre fod, så hans venstre), at hun aldrig før havde set støvler af lige den facon. Og læderet var det fineste i verden. Det meste læder var blot brunt papir og pap. Fornøjet med sig selv betragtede han sin fod, der stadig var i luften. De var nået, følte hun, til en solbeskinnet ø, hvor freden havde hjemme, hvor sundt vid herskede, og hvor solen aldrig holdt op med at skinne: de gode støvlers saligheds ø. Hun følte en varme for ham. »Lad os nu se, om De kan binde en knude,« sagde han. Han viftede hendes svage metode væk med foragt og demonstrerede sin egen opfindelse. Bandt man den én gang, ville den aldrig gå op. Tre gange knyttede han hendes sko; tre gange løste han den op igen.

english: But why did they have to come like _that_? She could not help feeling annoyed with them. They might have come more cheerfully; they might have given him what she, now that they were leaving, would have no chance to give him. For she felt a sudden emptiness, a frustration. Her feeling had come too late. There it was, ready, but he no longer needed it. He had turned into a very distinguished elderly man who had no need of her whatsoever. She felt snubbed. He slung a knapsack over his shoulders. He handed out the parcels—there were a number of them, badly tied, in brown paper. He sent Cam for a cloak. He looked every inch a leader getting ready for an expedition. Then, wheeling around, he led the way down the path with his firm military step, in those wonderful boots, carrying brown paper parcels, his children following him. They looked, she thought, as if fate had given them over to some stern undertaking, and they went to meet it, still young enough to be drawn along obediently in their father’s wake, but with a paleness in their eyes that made her feel they were silently suffering something beyond their years. So they passed the edge of the lawn, and it seemed to Lily that she was watching a procession go by, drawn on by some pressure of shared feeling which made it—faltering and flagging as it was—a little company bound together, and strangely impressive to her. Politely, but very distantly, Mr. Ramsay raised his hand and saluted her as they passed.
danish_before_fix: Men hvorfor skulle de komme på _den_ måde? Hun kunne ikke lade være med at føle sig irriteret på dem. De kunne have været mere muntre; de kunne have givet ham det, hun, nu da de var på vej af sted, ikke ville få chancen for at give ham. For hun følte en pludselig tomhed, en frustration. Hendes følelse var kommet for sent. Dér var den, parat, men han trængte ikke længere til den. Han var blevet til en meget fornem ældre mand, der slet ikke havde brug for hende. Hun følte sig afvist. Han slyngede en rygsæk over skuldrene. Han uddelte pakkerne — der var en del af dem, dårligt bundet ind i brunt papir. Han sendte Cam efter en kappe. Han så ud som en leder fra top til tå, der gjorde sig klar til en ekspedition. Så, vendt brat om, gik han i spidsen ned ad stien med sit faste, militære skridt, i de vidunderlige støvler, med brune papirpakker i hænderne og børnene efter sig. De så ud, tænkte hun, som om skæbnen havde overgivet dem til en streng opgave, og de gik den i møde, endnu unge nok til at lade sig trække lydigt med i deres fars kølvand, men med en bleghed i øjnene, der fik hende til at føle, at de i stilhed led noget, der ligger hinsides deres år. Så de passerede kanten af plænen, og det forekom Lily, at hun så en procession gå forbi, draget frem af et pres af fælles følelse, der gjorde den — vaklende og slappende som den var — til et lille selskab, bundet sammen og besynderligt imponerende for hende. Høfligt, men meget fjernt løftede hr. Ramsay hånden og hilste hende, idet de gik forbi.

english: But what a face, she thought, and at once the sympathy she had not been asked to give began troubling her, looking for a way out. What had made it like that? Thinking, night after night, she supposed—about the reality of kitchen tables, she added, remembering the symbol Andrew had given her when she was vague about what Mr. Ramsay actually thought about. (He had been killed instantly by a splinter of shell, she reminded herself.) The kitchen table was something visionary and austere; something bare, hard, not decorative. There was no color to it; it was all edges and angles; it was uncompromisingly plain. But Mr. Ramsay always kept his eyes fixed on it, never let himself be distracted or fooled, until his face too became worn and ascetic and shared in this unadorned beauty which impressed her so deeply. Then, she recalled (standing where he had left her, holding her brush), worries had worn at it—less nobly. He must have had his doubts about that table, she supposed: whether the table was a real table; whether it was worth the time he gave it; whether he was able, after all, to find it. He had had doubts, she felt, or he would have asked less of people. That was what they talked about late at night sometimes, she suspected; and then the next day Mrs. Ramsay looked tired, and Lily flew into a rage with him over some absurd little thing. But now he had nobody to talk to about that table, or his boots, or his knots; and he was like a lion seeking whom he might devour, and his face had that touch of desperation, of exaggeration, which alarmed her and made her pull her skirts around her. And then, she recalled, there was that sudden revival, that sudden flare (when she praised his boots), that sudden return of energy and interest in ordinary human things. That too passed and changed (for he was always changing, and hid nothing) into that other, final phase which was new to her, and which had, she admitted, made her ashamed of her own irritability. It seemed then as if he had shed his worries and ambitions, and the hope of sympathy and the desire for praise; as if he had entered some other region and was being drawn on, as if by curiosity, in silent conversation, whether with himself or with someone else, at the head of that little procession, out of one’s reach. An extraordinary face! The gate banged.

Tænkning, nat efter nat, formodede hun — om køkkenbordenes virkelighed, tilføjede hun, mindet om det symbol, Andrew havde givet hende, dengang hun var uklar over, hvad hr. Ramsay egentlig tænkte på. (Han var blevet dræbt øjeblikkeligt af et granatsplinter, mindede hun sig selv om.) Køkkenbordet var noget visionært og asketisk; noget bart, hårdt, ikke dekorativt. Der var ingen farve ved det; det var alt sammen kanter og vinkler; det var ubønhørligt enkelt. Men hr. Ramsay holdt altid blikket fæstnet på det, lod sig aldrig distrahere eller narre, indtil hans ansigt også blev slidt og asketisk og fik del i denne uprydede skønhed, der gjorde så dyb et indtryk på hende. Så, huskede hun (stående hvor han havde forladt hende, med sin pensel i hånden), havde bekymringer nagt det — mindre ædelt. Han måtte have haft sine tvivl om det bord, formodede hun: om bordet var et virkeligt bord; om det var den tid værd, han gav det; om han i det hele taget var i stand til at finde det. Han havde haft tvivl, følte hun, ellers ville han have krævet mindre af folk. Det var, hvad de talte om sent om aftenen nogle gange, mistænkte hun; og så så fru Ramsay træt ud næste dag, og Lily fór i totterne på ham over en eller anden absurd lille ting. Men nu havde han ingen at tale med om det bord eller sine støvler eller sine knuder; og han var som en løve, der søger, hvem den kan opsluge, og hans ansigt havde det anstrøg af fortvivlelse, af overdrivelse, som skræmte hende og fik hende til at trække sine skørter om sig. Og så, huskede hun, var der den pludselige genopvækkelse, det pludselige blus (da hun roste hans støvler), den pludselige tilbagekomst af energi og interesse for almindelige menneskelige ting. Også det gik over og forandrede sig (for han forandrede sig altid og skjulte intet) til den anden, endelige fase, som var ny for hende, og som, indrømmede hun, havde fået hende til at skamme sig over sin egen pirrelighed. Det var da, som om han havde aflagt sine bekymringer og ambitioner og håbet om medfølelse og længslen efter ros; som om han var trådt ind i en anden egn og blev draget videre, som af nysgerrighed, i tavs samtale, enten med sig selv eller med en anden, i spidsen for den lille procession, uden for ens rækkevidde. Et ekstraordinært ansigt! Lågen smækkede.

english: So they’re gone, she thought, sighing with relief and disappointment. Her sympathy seemed to fly back into her face, like a bramble springing back. She felt strangely divided, as if one part of her were drawn out there—it was a still, hazy day; this morning the Lighthouse looked immensely far away—while the other part had planted itself stubbornly, solidly, here on the lawn. She saw her canvas as if it had floated up and set itself, white and uncompromising, right in front of her. With its cold stare it seemed to scold her for all this hurry and agitation, this foolishness and waste of emotion. It called her back sharply, and it spread through her mind first a peace, as her disorderly feelings (he had gone, and she had been so sorry for him, and she had said nothing) marched off the field; and then emptiness. She looked blankly at the canvas, with its uncompromising white stare; from the canvas to the garden. There was something (she stood screwing up her little Chinese eyes in her small puckered face), something she remembered in the way those lines related, cutting across, slicing down, and in the mass of the hedge with its green cave of blues and browns, which had stayed in her mind. It had tied a knot in her mind, so that at odd moments, without meaning to, as she walked along the Brompton Road in London, as she brushed her hair, she found herself painting that picture, running her eye over it, and untying the knot in her imagination. But there was all the difference in the world between this airy planning away from the canvas and actually taking up her brush and making the first mark.

english: “Like a work of art,” she repeated, looking from her canvas to the drawing-room steps and back again. She had to rest for a moment. And as she rested, looking vaguely from one to the other, the old question that was forever crossing the sky of the soul—the vast, general question which tended to take on a particular shape at moments like these, when she let go of faculties that had been under strain—stood over her, paused over her, darkened over her. What is the meaning of life? That was all—a simple question; one that tended to close in on you as the years went by. The great revelation had never come. Perhaps the great revelation never did come. Instead there were little daily miracles, illuminations, matches struck unexpectedly in the dark; here was one. This, that, and the other; herself and Charles Tansley and the breaking wave; Mrs. Ramsay bringing them together; Mrs. Ramsay saying “Life stand still here”; Mrs. Ramsay making something permanent out of the moment (just as Lily herself, in another sphere, tried to make something permanent out of the moment)—this had the nature of a revelation. In the midst of chaos there was shape; this eternal passing and flowing (she looked at the clouds going by and the leaves shaking) was struck into something stable. Life stand still here, Mrs. Ramsay said. “Mrs. Ramsay! Mrs. Ramsay!” she repeated. She owed this revelation to her.

english: Yes, the breeze was getting stronger. The boat heeled over; the water was cut sharply and fell away in green cascades, in bubbles, in waterfalls. Cam gazed down into the foam, into the sea and all the treasure it held, and its speed put her in a trance, and the bond between her and James went slack a little. It loosened slightly. How fast it goes, she began to think. Where are we going? The motion entranced her, while James steered grimly, his eye on the sail and the horizon. Yet as he steered, a thought began to come to him: he might get away; he might be done with all of it. They might land somewhere, and then be free. For a moment the two of them looked at each other and felt a lift of escape and exhilaration, from the speed and the change. But the breeze roused that same excitement in Mr. Ramsay, too. As old Macalister turned to cast his line over the side, he cried out loud, “We perished,” and then again, “each alone.” Then, in his usual spasm of shyness or remorse, he caught himself up and waved a hand at the shore.
danish_before_fix: Jo, brisen blev stærkere. Båden krængede; vandet blev skåret skarpt over og faldt bort i grønne kaskader, i bobler, i vandfald. Cam stirrede ned i skummet, ned i havet og al den skat, det rummede, og farten satte hende i trance, og båndet mellem hende og James slappedes lidt. Det løsnedes en anelse. Hvor det går hurtigt, begyndte hun at tænke. Hvor skal vi hen? Bevægelsen fortryllede hende, mens James styrede dystert med øjet på sejlet og horisonten. Men mens han styrede, begyndte en tanke at dukke op i ham: han kunne slippe væk; han kunne være færdig med det hele. De kunne lande et sted og så være frie. Et øjeblik så de to på hinanden og følte et løft af flugt og begejstring, fra farten og forandringen. Men brisen vakte den samme begejstring i hr. Ramsay. english: “But I beneath a rougher sea,” Mr. Ramsay murmured—a line from Cowper’s “The Castaway,” about a sailor drowned alone. He had found the house, and seeing it, he had seen himself there too, pacing the terrace alone. Up and down between the urns he was walking, and to himself he seemed very old and stooped. There in the boat he stooped, too, and hunched down, instantly playing his role—the role of a lonely man, widowed and bereft. That way he could summon up crowds of people who pitied him. Sitting in the boat, he put on a little play for himself, one that called for frailty and weariness and grief from him (he held up his hands and looked at how thin they were, to confirm the dream). Then, in abundance, women’s sympathy was handed to him, and he imagined how they would comfort him and feel for him. And catching in his dream some glimmer of the exquisite pleasure that women’s sympathy gave him, he sighed, and said softly and sadly,

english: And what name would she give him? her father kept on. When he was a small boy he had had a dog called Frisk. She’s going to give in, James thought, watching a certain look come over her face, a look he remembered. They look down at their knitting, or something, he thought. Then all at once they look up. He remembered a flash of blue, and then someone sitting with him laughed and gave in, and he was furious. It must have been his mother, he thought, in a low chair, with his father standing over her. He began to hunt through the endless series of impressions that time had laid down on his brain, softly, ceaselessly, leaf upon leaf, fold upon fold: scents, sounds; voices, harsh, hollow, sweet; lights going by, and brooms tapping; the wash and hush of the sea; how a man had marched up and down and stopped dead, standing upright over them. Meanwhile, he noticed, Cam was dabbling her fingers in the water, staring at the shore, saying nothing. No, she won’t give in, he thought; she’s not like that. Well, then, if Cam would not answer, he would leave her alone, Mr. Ramsay decided, and felt in his pocket for a book. But she did want to answer him. She longed, passionately, to shift whatever lay on her tongue and blocked it, and to say, Oh yes, Frisk. I’ll call him Frisk. She even wanted to ask, Was that the dog that found its own way across the moor? But however hard she tried, she could think of nothing like that to say—something fierce and faithful to the compact, yet which would pass her father, without James suspecting, a secret sign of the love she felt for him. For as she dabbled her hand (and just then Macalister’s boy caught a mackerel, and it lay kicking on the bottom of the boat with blood on its gills)—for as she looked at James, who kept his eyes on the sail without any feeling, or now and then glanced at the horizon for a second, she thought: you aren’t exposed to it—this pressure, this split feeling, this extraordinary temptation. Her father was searching his pockets; another second and he would have his book. For nobody drew her more than he did. His hands were beautiful to her, and his feet, and his voice, his words, his hurry, his temper, his strangeness, his passion, the way he would say straight out in front of everybody, we perish, each alone, and his remoteness. (He had opened his book.) But what was still unbearable, she thought, sitting up straight and watching Macalister’s boy pull the hook from another fish’s gills, was that crude blindness and tyranny of his. It had poisoned her childhood and stirred up bitter storms, so that even now she would wake at night shaking with rage, remembering some command of his, some insolence: “Do this,” “Do that”; his domination; his “Submit to me.”

Nu giver hun efter, tænkte James, mens han så et vist udtryk brede sig over hendes ansigt, et udtryk han huskede. De ser ned på deres strikketøj eller sådan noget, tænkte han. Så ser de pludselig op. Han huskede et glimt af blåt, og så lo en, der sad sammen med ham, og gav efter, og han blev rasende. Det måtte have været hans mor, tænkte han, i en lav stol, med hans far stående over hende. Han begyndte at lede gennem den endeløse række af indtryk, som tiden havde lagt ned på hans hjerne, blidt, uophørligt, blad på blad, fold på fold: dufte, lyde; stemmer, hårde, hule, bløde; lys der gik forbi, og koste der bankede; havets skvulp og hvisken; hvordan en mand var marcheret op og ned og var standset brat, rejst op over dem. Imens lagde han mærke til, at Cam dyppede fingrene i vandet, stirrede mod kysten og ikke sagde noget. Nej, hun giver ikke efter, tænkte han; sådan er hun ikke. Nå, men hvis Cam ikke ville svare, ville han lade hende være, besluttede hr. Ramsay og famlede i lommen efter en bog. Men hun ville gerne svare ham. Hun længtes, lidenskabeligt, efter at flytte det, der lå på hendes tunge og spærrede, og sige: Åh jo, Frisk. Jeg kalder den Frisk. Hun ville endda spørge: Var det den hund, der fandt hjem over heden på egen hånd? Men hvor hårdt hun end prøvede, kunne hun ikke finde på noget af den slags at sige — noget heftigt og tro mod pagten, men som ville række hendes far, uden at James anede det, et hemmeligt tegn på den kærlighed, hun nærede til ham. For mens hun dyppede sin hånd (og netop da fik Macalisters dreng en makrel, og den lå og sprællede på bunden af båden med blod på gællerne) — for mens hun så på James, som holdt blikket på sejlet uden nogen følelse eller en gang imellem et øjeblik kiggede mod horisonten, tænkte hun: du er ikke udsat for det — dette pres, denne splittede følelse, denne ekstraordinære fristelse. Hendes far søgte i sine lommer; et sekund til, og han ville have sin bog. For ingen drog hende mere end han. Hans hænder var smukke for hende, og hans fødder, og hans stemme, hans ord, hans hastværk, hans hidsighed, hans mærkelighed, hans lidenskab, den måde han midt foran alle sammen kunne sige lige ud, vi omkommer, hver for sig, og hans afsides væsen. (Han havde åbnet sin bog.) Men det, der stadig var uudholdeligt, tænkte hun, mens hun satte sig op og så Macalisters dreng trække krogen ud af en anden fisks gæller, var hans råa blindhed og tyranni. Det havde forgiftet hendes barndom og vakt bitre storme, så hun selv nu kunne vågne om natten og ryste af raseri, når hun huskede et eller andet påbud fra ham, en eller anden uforskammethed: »Gør dét,« »Gør hint«; hans herredømme; hans »Underkast dig mig.«
